description: Pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Iona, Taize and Walsingham; Christmas and Easter; mission and Christian Aid.
content_html:
What Is Christian Pilgrimage?

Pilgrimage is a journey to a place that holds special religious significance. Christians have gone on pilgrimage since the early centuries of the Church. Motivations vary: to deepen faith, to seek healing, to do penance, to feel connected to events in Christian history, or simply to mark an important moment in life. Not all Christians agree that pilgrimage is necessary — many Protestants argue that God is present everywhere and can be worshipped anywhere; there is no need to travel to a special place. Catholics and Orthodox Christians tend to give greater emphasis to pilgrimage as a spiritually valuable practice.

Luke 2:41–43 records the family of Jesus travelling to Jerusalem for the Passover festival each year — showing that pilgrimage was part of Jesus’s own Jewish heritage. The young Jesus stays behind in the Temple, and his parents find him there — a story that affirms the significance of Jerusalem as a holy place associated with Jesus.

Key Fact

Edexcel specifies four Christian pilgrimage sites: Jerusalem (holy city — site of the Last Supper, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension of Jesus; the Via Dolorosa and Church of the Holy Sepulchre are key destinations); Iona (island off west Scotland — site of St Columba’s Celtic monastery, founded c.563 AD; the Iona Community promotes prayer, justice and spiritual renewal); Taizé (village in Burgundy, France — home of an ecumenical monastic community founded by Brother Roger Schutz in 1940, attracting young Christians worldwide for prayer, music and reconciliation); Walsingham (Norfolk, England — site of a Marian shrine since 1061, popular with Catholics and some Anglicans; pilgrims walk the “Holy Mile” to the Slipper Chapel).

Arguments for pilgrimage: Sacred places provide a powerful encounter with the history of faith; the effort of the journey mirrors the spiritual life; meeting other pilgrims builds community. For Catholics visiting Jerusalem, walking the Via Dolorosa (the route Jesus walked to the cross) is a profound act of meditation on the Passion. For young people at Taizé, the community’s simple, repetitive chants and silence offer something many do not find in regular parish worship. Arguments against pilgrimage: Many Protestant Christians (following the Reformation’s rejection of “holy places” as theologically significant) argue that God’s presence is not concentrated in physical locations. Jesus himself said “God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth” (John 4:24). Money spent on pilgrimage could be better given to the poor. The Reformers were suspicious of indulgences (spiritual credits) historically associated with pilgrimage. Accordingly, many evangelical and Baptist Christians do not practise pilgrimage.

Christian Festivals: Christmas and Easter

The Christian calendar is structured around two major festivals. Christmas celebrates the incarnation — God becoming human in the birth of Jesus. The season of Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas and is a time of preparation and waiting. Christians use Advent candles, calendars and special services to mark the season. On Christmas Day, churches across all denominations celebrate the birth of Jesus, reading Luke 2 (the nativity) and reflecting on the significance of the incarnation.

Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar — the celebration of the resurrection of Jesus. The season of Holy Week runs from Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem) through Maundy Thursday (Last Supper) and Good Friday (the crucifixion) to Easter Sunday (the resurrection). 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 is Paul’s definitive statement on the resurrection’s importance: “If Christ has not been raised, our preaching is useless and so is your faith.” Paul argues that the resurrection is not optional for Christian belief but foundational to it.

Mission, Evangelism and the Future of the Church

Mission is the Church’s calling to bring the good news of Jesus to the world. Evangelism is one aspect of mission — actively proclaiming the faith to those who have not heard it. Mark 16:9–20 (the “longer ending” of Mark, noted by scholars as a later addition) records the Great Commission — “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation.” Note: Edexcel specifies this passage for this section on the future of the Church; students should be aware it is the longer ending of Mark, which textual scholars regard as a later addition not found in the earliest manuscripts.

Christians engage in mission through local outreach (food banks, street pastors, community cafes), national programmes (Alpha courses, school chaplaincy) and global mission organisations. The growth of Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, particularly in Africa, Latin America and Asia, represents one of the most significant developments in 21st-century mission.

Key Fact

1 Peter 5:1–4 addresses church elders (leaders), calling them to “be shepherds of God’s flock” not for financial gain or by domineering over others, but as examples. This passage grounds Christian leadership in servanthood. Matthew 25:31–46 (the Parable of the Sheep and Goats) is the foundation for Christian social action: Jesus identifies himself with “the least of these” — the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick and imprisoned. Christian Aid is a development and humanitarian organisation funded by UK and Irish churches. It works in the world’s most vulnerable communities to end poverty and injustice, grounding its work in Matthew 25 and 1 Corinthians 13 (Paul’s description of love: patient, kind, not self-seeking).

Ecumenism is the movement toward Christian unity across denominations. The World Council of Churches (founded 1948) and local “Churches Together” groups in the UK represent the ecumenical movement in practice. Taizé is an explicitly ecumenical community — its founding vision was that Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox would pray together. The local parish is the primary point of ecumenical engagement in most towns and cities. The persecuted Church refers to Christians facing imprisonment, violence or death for their faith — organisations such as Open Doors estimate that over 365 million Christians worldwide face high levels of persecution. The Taizé Community’s emphasis on reconciliation speaks directly to contexts of persecution and conflict.
exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark source question on pilgrimage or festivals, you have strong options: “Luke 2:41–43 records Jesus’s family travelling to Jerusalem for the Passover, showing pilgrimage as part of Jesus’s own heritage” is a named source that earns the 5th mark. “1 Corinthians 15:12–34 states that if Christ has not been raised, faith is useless” earns the 5th mark for Easter questions. For Christian Aid questions, cite “Matthew 25:31–46” or “1 Corinthians 13” by name. For 12-mark Discuss questions about pilgrimage or mission, the alternative point of view is often the Protestant argument that God is omnipresent and doesn’t require physical travel — develop this with at least two reasons and a named source, not just one sentence. Note: Mark 16:9–20 is the ‘longer ending’ of Mark, considered by textual scholars to be a later addition — Edexcel specifies it for the future-of-the-Church section only. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of ‘pilgrimage’, ‘ecumenism’, ‘evangelism’ and ‘Eucharist’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edexcel specifies four pilgrimage sites: Jerusalem (crucifixion/resurrection), Iona (Celtic Christian community), Taizé (ecumenical youth community, France) and Walsingham (Marian shrine, Norfolk). Not all Christians support pilgrimage — many Protestants argue God is equally present everywhere.
  • Christmas celebrates the incarnation (preceded by Advent); Easter is the most important festival, celebrating the resurrection — 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 makes clear the resurrection is foundational. Holy Week leads from Palm Sunday through Good Friday to Easter Sunday.
  • The Church’s mission and social action are grounded in Matthew 25:31–46 and 1 Corinthians 13; Christian Aid works to end poverty; 1 Peter 5:1–4 calls church leaders to shepherd, not dominate; ecumenism seeks unity among denominations.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Christians go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- To deepen their faith through visiting places associated with Jesus or Christian history.
- To seek healing, believing that sacred sites have spiritual power.
- To do penance — to show contrition for sins through the effort of the journey.
- To feel connected to the events of Christian history (e.g. walking the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem).
- To build community with other Christians through a shared experience.
Each point must be identifiably separate — do not award a mark for three sentences restating the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of Taize as a Christian pilgrimage site.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Taize is a village in Burgundy, France, home to an ecumenical monastic community founded by Brother Roger Schutz in 1940.
- It attracts young Christians from around the world for prayer, meditation, and reconciliation.
- Its worship is characterised by simple, repetitive chants and extended periods of silence.
- It is specifically ecumenical — Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox pray together, making it a symbol of Christian unity.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian Aid puts Christian teaching into practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Christian Aid works to end poverty in the world's most vulnerable communities, grounded in Jesus's teaching in Matthew 25:31-46 that serving 'the least of these' is serving Christ himself. By providing emergency relief and long-term development projects, Christian Aid treats those in need as bearers of divine dignity.
- Christian Aid campaigns for justice and systemic change — not only meeting immediate needs but challenging the structural causes of poverty such as unjust trade laws and climate change. This reflects 1 Corinthians 13's description of love as concerned for the welfare of others, not self-seeking.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Easter is the most important festival in the Christian year, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus, which Paul calls the foundation of Christian faith: without the resurrection, faith is 'futile' and Christians are 'still in their sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17). If Jesus did not rise, the cross is simply a tragedy rather than a saving event. Easter is more important than Christmas because it validates the incarnation — the resurrection proves that Jesus was who he claimed to be.
- Easter is the basis of Christian hope for life after death: because Jesus rose, Christians believe they too will rise. The resurrection is not just a historical claim but the reason Christians can face death without despair. 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ 'the first-fruits of those who have fallen asleep' — the first of many to be raised.

The 5th mark: name a source — '1 Corinthians 15:12-34', 'Luke 24', or another specific passage. Paraphrase without a named passage does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Pilgrimage is not necessary for Christians today.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support (pilgrimage is not necessary):
- Protestant Christians argue that God is omnipresent: Jesus said 'God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth' (John 4:24). There is no biblical command to visit specific physical places — the New Testament church is built on a relationship with the living Christ, not on sacred geography.
- Money spent on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela or Jerusalem could be given directly to the poor, which Jesus commanded more explicitly (Matthew 25:31-46). Pilgrimage can be a way of performing visible religious devotion without addressing the deeper ethical demands of the Gospel.
- The Reformation rejected the idea that sacred places confer special spiritual benefits, arguing that this was a form of works-righteousness — trying to earn spiritual credit by visiting the right places rather than trusting in grace alone.

Arguments against (pilgrimage has value):
- Sacred places provide a powerful encounter with the history of faith: visiting Jerusalem and walking the Via Dolorosa gives Christians a physical and emotional connection to the events of Holy Week that transforms understanding of the Passion. Luke 2:41-43 shows Jesus's own family making pilgrimage to Jerusalem each year.
- Taize attracts hundreds of thousands of young Christians annually because its combination of communal prayer, music and ecumenical encounter meets a spiritual need that local parish worship often cannot. The fruit of these pilgrimages — revitalised faith, ecumenical relationships, renewed commitment to justice — is evidence of their value.
- Even for Protestants who reject the idea of inherently sacred places, the discipline of pilgrimage — setting aside time, travelling, meeting other believers — is a powerful spiritual practice consistent with biblical calls to seek God intentionally.

SPaG: 'pilgrimage', 'ecumenism', 'evangelism' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the local church serves its community.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The local church provides practical support for those in need: food banks, street pastors, community cafes and debt counselling services are run by churches across the UK. This is grounded in 1 Peter 5:1-4's call to pastoral care and in Matthew 25:31-46's identification of Jesus with the vulnerable.
- The local church provides a centre of community identity and worship: services, youth groups, parent-and-toddler groups and community events make the church a gathering place for people of all ages. Ecumenical partnerships between denominations ('Churches Together' groups) strengthen this local presence, giving the church a unified voice in the community.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

options: The resurrection is symbolic, not literal
Only those who go on pilgrimage will be raised
If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile
The resurrection happened to all believers at baptism

Scottish island with a Celtic monastery founded by St Columba c.563 AD
Norfolk shrine associated with Mary — popular with Catholic and Anglican pilgrims

flashcard_questions.a: An ecumenical community in France using simple chants and silence, attracting young Christians worldwide.

Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday — including Maundy Thursday (Last Supper) and Good Friday (crucifixion).

flashcard_questions.a: Serving 'the least of these' (hungry, sick, imprisoned) is serving Jesus himself.

flashcard_questions.a: A church-funded development charity — grounded in Matthew 25:31-46 and 1 Corinthians 13.

flashcard_questions.a: Leaders should shepherd God's flock willingly, as examples — not for money or by dominating others.

glossary_terms.definition: A journey to a place of special religious significance, undertaken as an act of devotion, penance, healing or spiritual growth.
The four-week period of preparation and anticipation before Christmas, beginning the fourth Sunday before Christmas Day.
The week before Easter Sunday, including Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday and Good Friday — marking the last week of Jesus's life.
The Friday before Easter Sunday, marking the crucifixion and death of Jesus.
The Church's calling to spread the Christian faith to people who have not heard or accepted it.
Active proclamation and sharing of the Christian faith with the intention of inviting others to become Christians.
The movement seeking visible unity among the world's separated Christian churches.
